title: Regulated Crypto Custody: Compliance in Digital Asset Security
summary: Institutions evaluating regulated custody today have more guidance than they did only a few years ago. The framework is still evolving, and due diligence remains essential.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


Institutions have more guidance around digital asset custody than they did a few years ago, but the regulatory framework continues to evolve.


-


Early crypto custody models did not fully address the legal and operational responsibilities institutions brought into the market.


-


Institutions evaluate custody providers based on legal protections, security controls, asset segregation, and reporting capabilities.


-


Regulated custody increasingly serves as the foundation for broader institutional digital asset activity.


-


BitGo Bank & Trust, National Association combines federally supervised custody with infrastructure designed to support institutional requirements.


Custody has always been part of the foundation that allows financial markets to function. Institutions do not simply buy assets and hope for the best. They rely on established arrangements that define who holds those assets, what protections apply to them, and what happens if something goes wrong.


Digital assets developed differently. Early participants often relied on exchanges that combined custody with trading, lending, and settlement in a single environment. As institutions began exploring digital assets, they brought expectations shaped by years of operating on behalf of clients, investors, and beneficiaries. The ability to safeguard assets securely remained essential, but institutions also needed confidence that existing responsibilities could still be met.


That gap shaped the development of regulated custody. Rather than replacing the security principles that emerged in crypto's early years, regulated custody built on them by adding the legal protections and operational standards institutions already relied on elsewhere in financial services. Institutions evaluating custody today have more guidance than they did just a few years ago, along with a clearer framework for deciding which providers can support their needs.


## Why Institutions Needed a Different Custody Model


In crypto's early years,[custody](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/qualified-custody-vs-self-custody/) was often defined by a simple principle: whoever controlled the private keys controlled the assets. For individuals participating directly in the market, that approach aligned with the ideals of self-custody and personal ownership that shaped the industry's early development.


Institutions entered under different circumstances. They were not safeguarding assets solely for themselves. They were acting on behalf of clients, shareholders, beneficiaries, and investors, bringing obligations that existed long before digital assets emerged.


Protecting private keys remained important, but it was only one part of the equation. Institutions also needed confidence that client assets would remain separate from a provider's own balance sheet, that records could support audits and financial reporting, and that responsibilities were clearly defined if something went wrong. Questions that traditional markets had spent decades answering suddenly had to be addressed in a digital asset context.


Regulated custody emerged to address those questions. Institutions needed clarity around who held the assets, how ownership records would be maintained, and what legal protections would apply if a custodian encountered operational or financial distress. The goal extended beyond preventing unauthorized access. Custody arrangements needed to support the oversight, accountability, and continuity institutions already expected from providers entrusted with safeguarding assets on behalf of others.


Holding assets securely was necessary. Demonstrating how those assets were protected, how ownership could be verified, and what safeguards existed during periods of stress mattered just as much.


## The Custody Framework Is Taking Shape


For years, institutions evaluating digital asset custody had limited guidance on how existing safeguards applied to a new asset class. Many organizations were left to interpret evolving expectations on their own, contributing to a cautious approach toward the market.


The SEC's[decision](https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/publications/deloitte/heads-up/2025/sec-rescinds-sab-121-issues-sab-122-crypto-cryptocurrency) to rescind Staff Accounting Bulletin 121 and replace it with SAB 122 removed one of the obstacles institutions had identified most often. Under SAB 121, entities safeguarding digital assets generally recorded those assets and corresponding liabilities on their own balance sheets. Critics argued that treatment made custody unnecessarily expensive and discouraged participation. SAB 122 did not create a comprehensive custody framework, but it eliminated an accounting approach many institutions viewed as a barrier to offering custody services.


Other developments provided clearer points of reference. In late 2025, the OCC granted approvals for several digital asset custodians to operate within the national trust bank framework, including[conditional approval](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/bitgo-secures-occ-approval/) for BitGo Bank & Trust, National Association. For institutions already accustomed to regulated financial providers, those approvals placed digital asset custody within supervisory structures defined by examinations, governance expectations, and established risk-management practices.


The[GENIUS Act](https://www.richmondfed.org/banking/banker_resources/news_flash/2025/20251118_genius_act) , passed by Congress in 2025, established the first federal framework for payment stablecoins, setting expectations around reserve backing, redemption rights, disclosures, and oversight while agencies continue developing and implementing rules. Although focused on stablecoins, the legislation reflected a broader shift toward defining how critical parts of digital asset infrastructure should operate rather than leaving institutions to navigate uncertain expectations on their own.


The[Digital Asset Market Clarity Act](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12583) remains under consideration. If enacted, it would further define how customer assets should be held and reinforce the role of qualified custodians in certain parts of the market.


Institutions evaluating regulated custody today have more guidance than they did only a few years ago. The framework is still evolving, and due diligence remains essential. Even so, these developments have given institutions clearer expectations around custody practices, oversight, and the legal protections supporting customer assets. Assessing custody providers increasingly involves applying familiar standards rather than interpreting an entirely unfamiliar environment.


## How Institutions Evaluate Custody Providers Today


As institutions have gained experience[evaluating regulated custody providers](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/what-to-look-for-in-an-institutional-crypto-custody-provider/) , due diligence has increasingly resembled the reviews applied to other financial service relationships.


The process often starts with the custody arrangement itself. Institutions want to understand who legally holds the assets, what obligations define that relationship, and whether the provider operates within a supervisory framework aligned with their own requirements. Those answers shape what protections apply to client assets and whether the arrangement can satisfy expectations from boards, investors, and regulators.


Security reviews go beyond asking whether assets can be protected today. Institutions examine how keys are generated and recovered, how[multi-party computation](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/mpc-crypto-wallets-multi-party-computation-security/) (MPC) is implemented, and how transaction approvals move through the organization. Controls that work well with a small team and predictable activity may be tested differently as transaction volumes increase, approval groups expand, or urgent requests arrive outside normal business hours.


Institutions also evaluate how custody arrangements perform under stress. Asset segregation, the separation of custody from other business activities, bankruptcy-remote structures, and insurance coverage help clarify whether clients retain clear rights to their assets if a provider encounters financial distress. These safeguards may attract little attention when markets are calm. Their value becomes much clearer during periods of volatility, when institutions need confidence that protections will perform as intended.


The review does not end with policies and process diagrams. Institutions increasingly expect evidence that controls operate as intended. SOC reports, proof-of-reserves reporting, reconciliation records, and documentation that supports audits, examinations, and investor reporting obligations all help demonstrate that safeguards extend beyond written policies.


Many of the questions institutions ask today would sound familiar in other areas of financial services. Who holds the assets? How are they protected? What happens if conditions deteriorate? What evidence exists to support those answers? Digital assets introduce new technologies, but they have not changed the need for accountability.


## How BitGo Addresses Institutional Expectations


BitGo has provided regulated institutional digital asset[custody](https://www.bitgo.com/products/qualified-custody/) since 2013. In 2025, the OCC granted approval for BitGo Bank & Trust, National Association to convert from a South Dakota-chartered trust company to a federally chartered national trust bank. For institutions accustomed to working with regulated financial providers, that structure places digital asset custody within a framework shaped by examinations, oversight, and established governance expectations.


The same questions institutions ask during due diligence apply in practice. Client assets held by BitGo Bank & Trust, National Association are maintained in regulated, bankruptcy-remote cold storage backed by up to $250 million in insurance coverage. MPC-based key management is designed to reduce single points of failure, while policy controls help institutions enforce approval requirements that reflect internal authorities and separation-of-duties expectations.


Security alone is rarely enough. Institutions also need evidence that controls operate as intended. BitGo’s[SOC 1 Type II and SOC 2 Type II](https://www.vanta.com/collection/soc-2/soc-1-vs-soc-2-which-one-do-you-need) certifications support examinations, audits, and oversight processes by helping organizations demonstrate that controls operate as intended to boards, investors, and regulators.


Custody also underpins a growing range of institutional activities. As organizations expand into trading, settlement, staking, treasury operations, and stablecoin initiatives, they often prefer extending existing controls rather than creating separate governance processes for each new activity. A common custody foundation can help institutions apply consistent standards for safekeeping, reporting, and oversight across their broader digital asset operations.


Custody was one of the first questions institutions had to answer when evaluating digital assets. The choices made at that stage often shape how organizations govern assets, manage risk, satisfy oversight requirements, and pursue new opportunities.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is regulated crypto custody?


Regulated crypto custody refers to the safekeeping of digital assets by a provider operating under an established supervisory framework. For institutions, it combines asset protection with clear legal responsibilities, oversight, and controls designed to safeguard client assets.


### What is a qualified custodian in crypto?


A qualified custodian is an entity authorized to safeguard client assets under applicable regulatory standards. In digital assets, qualified custodians often provide protections related to asset segregation, recordkeeping, examinations, and oversight that institutions rely on when holding assets on behalf of others.


### Why does regulated custody matter for institutions?


Institutions are often responsible for assets held on behalf of clients, investors, or beneficiaries. Secure key management is important, but institutions also need clear accountability, operational controls, and protections that can withstand scrutiny from boards, auditors, regulators, and investors.


### What changed when SAB 121 was replaced?


The SEC replaced Staff Accounting Bulletin 121 with SAB 122. SAB 121 generally required entities safeguarding digital assets to recognize those assets and corresponding liabilities on their balance sheets, which many institutions viewed as a barrier to offering custody services. SAB 122 removed that accounting treatment but did not establish a complete custody framework.


### Why is cold storage important for institutional digital asset custody?


Cold storage keeps digital assets offline when they are not actively being used, reducing exposure to internet-based threats. Institutions typically evaluate cold storage alongside key management practices, recovery procedures, and approval controls as part of a broader custody framework.


### How does MPC key management support custody security?


Multi-party computation (MPC) distributes key responsibilities across multiple parties or systems rather than relying on a single private key holder. This approach may reduce single points of failure and support governance models that require multiple approvals before assets move.


### How does regulated custody support broader digital asset activity?


Custody provides the foundation for many institutional activities, including trading, settlement, staking, treasury operations, and stablecoin initiatives. A strong custody framework helps organizations apply consistent controls and governance standards as their digital asset activities expand.
